Tell Schwab to Move $19,000 of Apple Stock to Your Son on December 30 and If the Shares Land January 4 the IRS Counts It as a 2027 Gift. This Year's Exclusion Is Gone for Good
sum: This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

A 71-year-old retired dentist has a plan for his son: $19,000 of Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL | AAPL Price Prediction) stock every year, the exact annual exclusion, with no paperwork. Say he gifts late this year. On December 30 he calls Charles Schwab (NYSE:SCHW), and the rep submits a transfer to his son’s account at another brokerage.
Markets close for New Year’s Day. Say the shares show up in his son’s account on January 4. A few weeks later, he sends 2027’s gift on schedule.
His CPA then gives him the bad news. Both gifts count as 2027 gifts. His 2026 exclusion expired unused at midnight on December 31.

The gift tax counts a gift on the date the donor gives up control. For stock, Treasury spells out that date. Under 26 CFR 25.2511-2(h)[1], when a donor gives shares to “his bank or broker as his agent” for transfer into the donee’s name, “the gift is completed on the date the stock is transferred on the books of the corporation.”

Schwab works for the father. Until the shares are registered to the son, the father still owns them. With brokerage shares, that registration happens when the shares post to the son’s account. What counts is the posting date.

Then the calendar takes over. Internal Revenue Code § 2503(b)(1)[2] excepts present-interest gifts “made to any person by the donor during the calendar year.” For 2026, Rev. Proc. 2025-32 sets that amount at $19,000 per recipient. The Code has no carryforward for an exclusion you didn’t use. Each year’s exclusion stands on its own and disappears when the year ends.

items.t: Robinhood, E*TRADE, Fidelity and Charles Schwab Reported Downtime as US Stocks Surge
sum: Several major US trading and financial platforms, including Robinhood, E*TRADE, Fidelity and Charles Schwab, have reportedly experienced service disruptions as retail traders rush into the stock market amid a sharp increase in trading activity. The reported outages coincided with a major market rally that added nearly $3 trillion to the US stock market after the opening bell, while Nvidia (NVDA) shares surged more than 30%.

According to information shared by Coin Bureau on X, multiple trading and finance applications were reporting downtime as market activity accelerated. The disruptions affected several widely used platforms, raising concerns about access to trading services during a period of heightened market volatility and strong investor participation.

Robinhood, E*TRADE, Fidelity and Charles Schwab were among the platforms identified in reports of widespread technical issues. The problems emerged as retail traders moved into US markets, with multiple financial applications reportedly experiencing downtime.

The reported disruptions highlight the importance of reliable digital infrastructure during periods of intense market activity. Retail investors increasingly markets depend on brokerage applications to monitor stock prices, manage portfolios and execute transactions. When these services become unavailable, users may face difficulties accessing their accounts or responding to rapidly changing market conditions.

However, the information shared by Coin Bureau did not specify the precise technical cause of the reported disruptions, the number of affected customers or how long the service interruptions lasted. It also did not establish whether all four platforms experienced identical problems.

The reported platform issues coincided with an exceptionally strong session for US equities. Nearly $3 trillion was added to the US stock market following the opening bell, according to the figures cited in Coin Bureau's post.

sum: XRP exchange-traded fund shares appeared in collateral baskets posted by JPMorgan and Bank of America to a Schwab money market fund, according to wealth coach Kamilah Stevenson.
In her latest YouTube episode, she argues that the reported holdings point to a less visible source of institutional demand: securities pledged against loans rather than bought for price exposure.
The distinction matters. Stevenson says Schwab did not buy XRP or the ETFs outright; its fund lent cash and received baskets of securities backing the transactions.
Citing monthly SEC disclosures, Stevenson identifies XRP ETF shares from Grayscale, Canary, Franklin and Bitwise among collateral supplied by the banks’ trading arms.
She puts their combined value at roughly $36,000 in April, $2 million in June and more than $8 million by August, an increase exceeding 200-fold.
Those figures remain claims presented in the video. The transcript does not specify the reporting year or filing identifiers, limiting verification of the sequence.

Stevenson acknowledges that the positions were small relative to the underlying loans. Their inclusion would demonstrate acceptance of particular ETF securities within collateral baskets, not necessarily an institutional commitment to holding XRP directly.

Stewart Cink’s lead shrinks to 3 entering Charles Schwab Cup final round
sum: Stewart Cink shot a 3-under-par 68 on Saturday to hold a three-stroke lead at the Charles Schwab Cup Championship in Phoenix, keeping him on track to defend both the tournament title and the season-long points crown.

Cink followed rounds of 63 and 65 with a less spectacular performance at Phoenix Country Club, reaching 17-under 196 through 54 holes. His six-shot advantage after the second round was trimmed by Zach Johnson and Australia’s Scott Hend, who finished the day tied for second at 14 under.
Cink, 53, struggled to sustain the momentum from his opening two rounds but preserved his lead with several timely recoveries.

“I mostly saved myself, got out of jail a couple times and I didn’t have a whole lot of offense going,” Cink said. “I played pretty good golf tee-to-green most of the day, but just the ball wasn’t really going in the hole much.”

Hend made the biggest move of the day, firing a 9-under 62 to climb from a tie for 15th into a share of second. The Australian started Saturday nine strokes behind Cink after opening with rounds of 67 and 70, but his surge put him squarely in contention entering the final 18 holes.

Johnson also closed the gap with a 7-under 64, his best round of the tournament. He was seven shots behind Cink after Friday’s play and now sits three back, leaving the two players who are still in the running for the Charles Schwab Cup separated by the same margin on the tournament leaderboard.

Johnson, a six-time winner during his rookie season on PGA Tour Champions, said he missed opportunities on the three par-5 holes despite an otherwise steady round. He will play alongside Sweden’s Freddie Jacobson (11 under) in Sunday’s penultimate pairing, with Hend joining Cink in the final group.

sum: When investors look at the discount broker industry today, fresh new names like Robinhood (HOOD +3.21%) probably get more attention than established names like Charles Schwab (SCHW -1.18%). That likely makes sense, given that Charles Schwab is one of the oldest companies in the sector. However, it would be a mistake to dismiss this financial giant. Here's how Schwab is quietly benefiting from the retail trading boom that's underway.

In May 2026, Charles Schwab's customers held accounts worth $13.1 trillion dollars. That's a huge sum of money. For comparison's sake, Robinhood's total platform assets amounted to "only" $344 billion. That's not meant to be a put-down to Robinhood, which is a much younger company and has achieved impressive things in a very short period of time. It is meant to show just how large Charles Schwab's business really is. In fact, it was one of the companies that helped Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +8.62%) go public.

It is easier to grow a small business, but that doesn't mean Charles Schwab isn't growing. The company's customer assets increased 27% year over year in May. That's a massive increase, helped along by rising stock prices and new accounts. According to the financial giant, "New brokerage accounts opened during the month totaled 461,000, an increase of 37% versus May 2025."

Every new account is a chance to earn more money from commissions, margin interest, and fee-generating services (from asset management services to the management fees earned from Schwab's own family of exchange-traded funds). On the trading front, the company hit a record daily average of 11.8 million trades in May. Margin loans, meanwhile, were up 38% from the end of 2025.

To be fair, Robinhood's growth opportunity is larger than Schwab's. But, as noted, it is easier to grow from a smaller base. There's a problem with that, as growth-enamored investors often push valuations to extreme levels. Notably, Robinhood's price-to-earnings ratio is 54x, while Schwab's is a far lower 19x.
Schwab is an industry giant that is quietly cashing in on the current trading boom. And you can buy it for less than half Robinhood's valuation.

sum: Charles Schwab released its first-quarter earnings report on April 16. Here’s Morningstar’s take on Schwab’s earnings and stock.

Schwab reported strong quarterly results, generating 16% sales growth, 38% growth in adjusted EPS, and attracting an outstanding $140 billion in net new client assets. Still, shares traded down by a mid-single-digit percentage during April 16 trading on cash-sorting fears.

Why it matters: Schwab is the low-cost operator in the retail brokerage and registered investment advisor custody space, and we believe it will emerge as a long-term winner as a result, regardless of the ultimate vehicle of customer monetization. We’ve seen the firm reinvent its model twice already; first with asset management through its first-party funds and mutual fund marketplace, and second through Schwab Bank.

- Concerns seem to center on JPMorgan Chase’s planned launch of an artificial intelligence cash management tool, alluded to in Jamie Dimon’s annual letter to shareholders. The comments seem to portray that product as evolutionary rather than revolutionary, with Dimon suggesting that high-net-worth clients are already adept at cash sorting and that competition for customer deposits is already intense.

- We don’t expect Schwab to see material pressure here. The rates paid on sweep deposits are very low—just 0.19% during the quarter—but also comprise less than 4% of customer assets. Customers seem to accept that low cash sweep rates are the ticket to admission for an otherwise free, robust ecosystem of services that Schwab provides. If the bank’s cost of funding were to tick up, those services would invariably need to be monetized in other ways.
The bottom line: As we digest results, we’ve raised our fair value estimate to $114 from $111, due to quarterly outperformance and a more constructive expected short-term interest rate environment.

Key stats: The firm’s $5.6 billion in revenue and $1.43 in adjusted EPS edged our respective $5.5 billion and $1.27 estimates, driven by better-than-expected 15% growth in asset management and 20% growth in trading revenue.

items.t: Schwab discloses it's set to levy new $5-per-client, per-block-trade fees that could balloon cost for RIA custody clients by thousands of dollars
sum: The RIA custodian has posted the coming fee on its pricing schedule -- raising questions related to trade-away policies, best execution and payment-for-order-flow.
Charles Schwab & Co. is adding a new, flat $5-per-account fee for select RIA trades that could cost advisors tens of thousands of dollars annually to use more complex investing strategies.

The fee, effective Mar. 2, will be levied on block orders – a best execution* trading practice for pricing large trades that require “special handling" from its trading desk, and don't go through its payment-for-order-flow algorithms, according to the its latest price guide.

Only block-trades made through Schwab’s bread-and-butter algorithms** remain free. The charge will apply if orders need manual support from Schwab’s staff trading desk, or require ‘complex’ algorithms, specific market conditions, or quotation requests from third-party desks.

“Schwab isn't just recovering commission revenue, they're re-architecting their entire custody model around operational efficiency while creating stronger incentives for advisors to utilize their integrated trading infrastructure," says Greg O'Gara, strategic advisor at Datos Insights.

“The $5 [per] account, block trading fee is one piece of a larger strategy to channel order flow through highly automated channels where operational costs are lowest and revenue capture, via payment-for-order-flow, is highest,” he adds, in an email.
The block-trade fee is “a strategic re-pricing of trading complexity," says Tim Welsh, a former Schwab director and now president of Larkspur, Calif., consultancy Nexus Strategy, in an email.
